title: Why Flower Needs Heat: Decarboxylation | The Bridge
description: The plant barely makes THC. It makes THCA, and heat does the rest. What decarboxylation is, what the lab measured, and what it means in a home oven.
lede: Raw flower and a finished edible are chemically different things. The step between them has a long name and a simple cause: heat.
html:
The plant barely makes THC. A 2016 study in Cannabis and Cannabinoid Research says it plainly: THC, CBD and CBG don't occur at significant concentrations in the plant. What cannabis produces is their acid forms, THCA, CBDA and CBGA, and those need one more step. The step is called decarboxylation, decarb for short.

What heat does

Acidic cannabinoids are thermally unstable. Expose them to heat through smoking, vaping or baking and they convert: THCA becomes THC. A lighter handles the job on the spot, which is why nobody thinks about it until they try to cook. It also happens slowly on its own. A 2021 review in Frontiers in Pharmacology notes some decarboxylation occurs with time at room temperature and with exposure to light.

Why it matters: THCA sits on the list of minor cannabinoids, and that same review reports none of them have been clinically demonstrated to act as psychotropic drugs. Skip the step in a low-heat recipe and much of what you paid for stays in its acid form.

What the lab measured

The 2016 team heated cannabis extracts in a vacuum oven and tracked how long THCA lasted:

  • Below 100°C (212°F): the reaction did not finish within 60 minutes.
  • 110°C (230°F): THCA approached zero in 30 minutes.
  • 130°C (266°F): 9 minutes.
  • 145°C (293°F): 6 minutes.

THCA converted cleanly, with no side reactions. CBDA and CBGA ran about half as fast, and some of that material went missing along the way, which the authors couldn't fully explain. Hotter isn't simply better, either. The paper cites earlier work in which THC peaked after five to ten minutes at 145°C and then fell off significantly, possibly through evaporation.

Those numbers are a map, not a recipe. They come from dried extract in a vial with the oxygen and light removed. Flower on a sheet pan in a home oven is a different situation, which is why our kitchen method goes a little longer: 240°F for 40 minutes, covered. Take that as a cautious starting point, not a lab result, and check your oven with a thermometer.

What you lose

Mostly the smell. A 2024 study in Molecules ran microwave-assisted decarb at 120°C for 30 minutes under a mild vacuum and collected the volatile compounds driven off. Those were mainly monoterpenes, the lighter aromatic molecules behind a lot of what you smell in the jar. In a kitchen they go into the air, so cover the pan and warn whoever you live with.

Why fat comes next

Converted THC still needs a ride into your food. Cannabinoids are lipophilic, meaning they move into fat. In a 2016 animal study, giving THC along with lipids raised rats' exposure about 2.5 times compared with a lipid-free formula, and the authors suggest a similar effect may be expected in people. That explains why the classic recipes start with butter or oil. It's also why an edible made with fat deserves respect.

Where you'll meet it on paper

This chemistry is written into the rules. New York's law defines Total THC as measured THC plus measured THCA multiplied by 0.877. And the new federal limit on hemp products counts THCA as well. Both are built on the same logic: what counts is what the acid can become.

One practical warning to finish. Once flower has been through the oven, handle it like a finished edible. Label it, lock it, and keep it far from anything anyone might snack on. If you want the wider picture of how all this works in the body, our Facts page is the place to go next.
